headline: Stories that stick.
intro: Tuesday. Vera asks the group the most natural question in the world — what did you do yesterday? Vera studied, Vera went to the cinema, and Vera\u2026 well, Vera ate. Every answer arrives in the Perfekt: a helper verb up front, a participle at the end.
scene: Im Kurs \u2014 "Was hast du gemacht?", Berlin
objective: See the two-part Perfekt frame before you begin.

headline: Stories that stick.
intro: The exam is over. In the café, the group compares how they prepared — who studied what, who read which book, who drank too much coffee. Every line is a haben-Perfekt: habe gelernt, hat gelesen, haben getrunken.
scene: Nach der Prüfung \u2014 im Café, Berlin
objective: See why haben is the default Perfekt helper.

headline: By the numbers.
intro: Third lesson, and two classmates finally get properly acquainted — names, ages, and the all-important phone-number swap. Emma reels off her digits; Tim needs them a little slower.
scene: Zahlen üben — Deutschkurs
objective: See the whole chapter at a glance before you begin.

headline: Stories that stick.
intro: Steffi is back from a short trip and the group wants every detail — where she flew, when she arrived, how long she stayed. Her whole story runs on sein-Perfekt: bin geflogen, ist angekommen, sind geblieben. Steffi, predictably, never left the sofa.
scene: Nach der Reise \u2014 im Kurs, Berlin
objective: See which verbs take sein in the Perfekt.

headline: Stories that stick.
intro: A lot happened yesterday. Wanda got a package, Wanda sold his old bike, and Wanda — forgot the whole class. As they catch up, every verb has a prefix: some keep ge- in the middle, some drop it completely.
scene: Vor dem Kurs \u2014 was gestern passiert ist, Berlin
objective: See how a prefix decides where ge- goes.

headline: Stories that stick.
intro: The class is planning a little party. Who is bringing the cake, who is calling Ronja, who has the music? As the group sorts out the jobs, every answer swaps the noun for a pronoun — ihn, sie, es, uns — so nobody has to repeat themselves.
scene: Kursplanung \u2014 das Fest, Berlin
objective: See how pronouns replace objects so you don\u2019t repeat nouns.

headline: Stories that stick.
intro: Weekend plans are up in the air. Carla wants to go out, Carla has a reason to study, and Carla \u2014 as ever \u2014 has an excuse. As they argue it out, every sentence gets glued to the next with und, aber, denn, deshalb and weil.
scene: Wochenendplanung \u2014 im Kurs, Berlin
objective: See the two connector groups and what they do to the verb.

headline: Stories that stick.
intro: Petra is throwing a birthday party and needs two messages: a casual WhatsApp to the gang and a formal email to invite Petra. As the group helps her write both, the difference between "Hi, kommst du?" and "Sehr geehrte Petra" comes alive.
scene: Eine Einladung schreiben \u2014 im Kurs, Berlin
objective: See the shape of a German message: salutation, body, closing.

headline: Stories that stick.
intro: Runa is back from a trip and has written a little holiday report. As she reads it out and the group reacts, almost every structure from Phase 4 surfaces \u2014 the Perfekt, war and hatte, pronouns, weil and deshalb \u2014 a perfect warm-up before the checkpoint.
scene: Vor dem Checkpoint \u2014 Annas Reisebericht, Berlin
objective: See how this checkpoint pulls all of A1 together.

headline: Stories that stick.
intro: It\u2019s gift time before the holidays. Alina gives the teacher flowers, Alina helps a classmate, and Alina\u2026 gives himself cake. Every "to whom?" puts the dative to work \u2014 dem, der, den \u2014 the case of the receiver.
scene: Geschenke vor den Ferien \u2014 im Kurs, Berlin
objective: See why German marks the receiver with a new case.

headline: Stories that stick.
intro: The group is planning a weekend trip to Munich. Who travels how, who they\u2019re staying with, how long they\u2019ve studied German \u2014 every answer rides on a dative preposition: mit dem Zug, bei der Tante, seit einem Jahr.
scene: Wochenendplanung \u2014 eine Reise, Berlin
objective: See the seven prepositions that always take the dative.

headline: Stories that stick.
intro: Franzi has a new flat and the gang is helping her move in. As they decide where the sofa, the lamp and the pictures go, the two-way prepositions come alive: putting things somewhere is accusative (Wohin?), and where they already sit is dative (Wo?).
scene: Umzug \u2014 Annas neue Wohnung, Berlin
objective: See how one question — Wohin? or Wo? — picks the case.

headline: Stories that stick.
intro: Meike is lost on the way to a new café and calls Meike for directions. As she walks him there \u2014 left, right, straight on, past the pharmacy \u2014 the location words and the everyday contractions (zum, zur, am, ins) do all the work.
scene: Auf dem Weg \u2014 eine Wegbeschreibung, Berlin
objective: See the location words and the everyday contractions at a glance.

headline: The right hello.
intro: David arrives at his Berlin language school and meets the receptionist, Frau Klein. A first, formal conversation — Sie, Herr and Frau — and he learns exactly when Germans switch to the friendly du.
scene: Anmeldung an der Sprachschule — Berlin
objective: See the whole chapter at a glance before you begin.

headline: Stories that stick.
intro: Nele needs an outfit for a party and drags the gang to a clothes shop. As they judge every jacket, dress and pair of shoes, the dative verbs do the talking: Das gefällt mir, das passt dir, der Mantel steht dir \u2014 and Nele, of course, helps no one.
scene: Im Kleidergesch\u00e4ft \u2014 ein Outfit f\u00fcr die Party, Berlin
objective: See which everyday verbs put the person in the dative.

headline: Stories that stick.
intro: Five minutes before class and nobody has what they need. Frau Sommer lends, Frau Sommer explains, Frau Sommer answers questions \u2014 and every favour swaps a name for a dative pronoun: Ich gebe ihr den Stift, ich erkläre es dir, das gehört ihm.
scene: Kurz vor dem Unterricht \u2014 im Kursraum, Berlin
objective: See how dative nouns become mir, dir, ihm, ihr …

headline: Stories that stick.
intro: The class hits a department store before the exam. Vreni needs a grammar book, Vreni can\u2019t choose a bag, and Vreni dithers over notebooks. Every choice is a "which one?" and a "this one" \u2014 welches Buch, diese Tasche, diesen Block.
scene: Im Kaufhaus \u2014 vor der Pr\u00fcfung, Berlin
objective: See that welcher/dieser just copy the der/die/das endings.

headline: Stories that stick.
intro: A rainy afternoon in the café. While they wait out the weather, the gang drifts into easy small talk \u2014 how\u2019s it going, what\u2019s the weekend look like, what\u2019s Berlin like \u2014 and Yvonne keeps slipping in sentences with man to explain how things are done in Germany.
scene: Im Caf\u00e9 \u2014 ein verregneter Nachmittag, Berlin
objective: Meet small talk and the impersonal pronoun man.

headline: Stories that stick.
intro: Frau Dr. Berg wakes up sick the day before the exam, so Frau Dr. Berg drags him to the doctor. The doctor examines him and fires off instructions \u2014 commands, what he may and may not do, and what he should take \u2014 while Frau Dr. Berg translates the rules and Frau Dr. Berg, predictably, protests.
scene: Beim Arzt \u2014 einen Tag vor der Pr\u00fcfung, Berlin
objective: See the three ways to steer people: command, may, should.

headline: Stories that stick.
intro: Still sick, Solveig misses class and phones Solveig to get the homework. The line is bad, Solveig talks too fast, and half the call is Solveig asking her to repeat, spell and slow down \u2014 exactly the phrases you need on a real German phone call.
scene: Ein Anruf \u2014 Max ruft Anna an, Berlin
objective: See the frame of a call: open, clarify, close.
